title: The Odyssey
subtitle: The Long Way Home
attribution: An original abridged adaptation of Homer’s Odyssey
description: The road home leads through a shore without morning.
intro: Some voices can only be heard after a farewell.
ending: He returned with a warning, and one promise to keep.
stageLabel: A pixel art retelling of the Odyssey

adaptationSource.title: Homer, Odyssey, Books X–XI
adaptationSource.note: Original abridged English narration and dialogue. Events are condensed for quiet episodic reading. Ritual sacrifice and deaths are represented without gore. The final conflict of Book XXIV is condensed to Athena intervening before renewed bloodshed.

steps.text: Odysseus was still telling Alcinous about the years before Calypso. His account continued on Circe’s island.
A year passed on Aeaea. The men recovered their strength. Then their thoughts turned toward home again.
Circe wanted to help them leave safely. Tiresias was a prophet: someone who could see dangers before they happened.
“You must first seek Tiresias, the prophet among the dead.”
“Another shore before Ithaca?”
“One that can tell you what waits on the way.”
Other sailors from their one surviving ship had rested on Aeaea too. Elpenor was the youngest of them.
Eurylochus brought sad news: Elpenor had fallen from the roof where he slept and died. The crew had lost another friend.
“We must remember him when we return.”
One place in their crew would stay empty. Ahead lay the edge of the living world.
Circe gave them directions to the dark shore. Odysseus, Eurylochus and Polites went back down the path to their ship.
Their remaining sailors were aboard too. Circe stayed on Aeaea while the same surviving ship carried them away.
They followed Circe’s directions across the sea. At last, they reached a cold shore near the world of the dead.

steps.text: They brought the ship to the dark shore. Eurylochus and Polites would wait aboard while Odysseus sought Tiresias.
Odysseus set out the offerings Circe had described to call the spirits of the dead. His companions waited with the ship.
Elpenor’s spirit appeared first. His body was still on Aeaea, and he wanted his friends to bury it when they returned.
“Do not leave me unburied. Raise my oar over the grave.”
“I will come back for you.”
Elpenor’s spirit faded, and Tiresias appeared. This was the prophet Circe had sent Odysseus to find.
Tiresias warned him about animals belonging to Helios, the god of the Sun. Killing them would bring danger to the crew.
“Leave the cattle of the Sun unharmed. If your men kill them, their ship will not bring them home.”
Odysseus listened. Knowing a danger, he was learning, did not mean he could keep everyone from it.
After Tiresias, his mother’s spirit appeared. Odysseus now learned that Anticleia had died in Ithaca while he was away.
“What brought you here? Was there no one to care for you?”
“There was care. There was also the long waiting for you.”
He reached for her. His arms closed on air. He could not quite accept that she was there and beyond him.
Twice more he had tried to hold her. Twice more she had slipped through his arms. At last, he listened.
“Penelope still waits. Your son has grown. Your father keeps to his fields.”
“Tell me what I can carry back.”
“The living are still there. Go to them.”
Next came Achilles, a warrior who had fought at Troy and died there. His spirit could tell Odysseus about this place.
“Even here, men honor you.”
“I would rather work a poor man’s field in the sunlight.”
The answer left no room for the songs Odysseus had expected. Glory had not made this shore warm.
“Tell me about my son.”
Odysseus told him of the young man’s courage at Troy. For a moment, Achilles stood straighter.
It was news of someone living that gave the dead warrior joy. Odysseus held that thought as he left.
The voices fell quiet. Odysseus left the offerings on the stones and followed the same path back to his waiting crew.
They sailed back to Aeaea to keep the promise to Elpenor. His body was still on the island.
Back on shore, the men went inland to bury Elpenor. Odysseus took his friend’s oar to mark the grave.

steps.text: Back on Aeaea, the men buried Elpenor. Odysseus brought the oar his companion had used at sea.
He planted it above the grave. There would be a mark for the man who had asked not to be forgotten.
“He was younger than my son.”
After the burial, Circe explained the dangers ahead. The Sirens sang to lure sailors away from their course and onto the rocks.
Wax would keep the crew from hearing the song. Ropes would keep Odysseus safely aboard, even if he wanted to follow it.
“You can listen to their song, if your men bind you to the mast. They must stop their ears.”
He left the oar standing. The warnings went with him; the grave stayed behind.
Ahead lay voices that would promise him everything. This time, he would have to ask not to be trusted.
